conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health specialist, and my job is simply to listen and understand how things have been feeling for you since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—often called the EPDS—which is a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us pick up on signs of depression, anxiety, and anything that might be weighing on you right now.  

Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, and there are no right or wrong answers—just your honest experience. I’ll ask 10 gentle questions about how you’ve felt over the past seven days; each one usually takes only a moment to answer. Whenever you’re ready, we can begin.  

To start: over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, laughing feels really hard lately. My sister sent me a silly meme yesterday and I could tell it was supposed to be funny, but I just kind of stared at it. I did chuckle once when the baby made a goofy face, but even that felt forced, like I had to remind myself “this is supposed to be fun.”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can’t remember the last time I laughed without forcing it.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much anymore. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like I’m just getting through the day. I still go through the motions, hoping maybe I’ll feel something, but the enjoyment part feels flat, like someone turned the volume way down.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it must be something I ate. When he wouldn’t settle last night, I kept replaying the day, convinced I’d overstimulated him. My partner says I’m doing fine, but in my head I’m always wondering, “What did I do wrong this time?”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s going to choke—even though she’s just fine. Or I’ll lie down and picture the stroller rolling into the street, or the crib slats somehow trapping her arm. I know it sounds crazy, but the thoughts just pop in and I can’t shut them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Uh-huh. A couple of nights this week I woke up gasping, heart pounding, sure something awful had happened to the baby. I’d rush to the crib and she’s sleeping peacefully, but in that moment it feels like the world is caving in. It takes me a long time to stop shaking and convince myself everything’s okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days. I’ll start with a simple plan—just fold the laundry, maybe wash a couple bottles—and then the baby cries, the pump parts need sterilizing, the trash is overflowing, and I feel like I’m drowning. I end up standing in the middle of the kitchen staring at everything, not even sure what to pick up first.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop spinning—running through everything I might’ve missed, worrying the baby will wake up any second. It takes me over an hour to fall asleep most nights, and even when I do, I jerk awake at every little sound, heart racing, sure something’s wrong.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a heavy cloud that settles in as soon as I open my eyes. Sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start leaking out for no real reason. I feel guilty because I know I’m supposed to be happy—she’s healthy, we’re safe—but the sadness is just… there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times. Yesterday I just sat in the rocker with her asleep on my chest and suddenly I was sobbing—quietly, so I wouldn’t wake her. Nothing specific triggered it; I just felt this wave of hopelessness crash over me. It passed after a few minutes, but I felt drained the rest of the day.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes… it’s crossed my mind once or twice this week. Nothing planned—just these quick, scary flashes like, “What if I weren’t here?” or “Maybe everyone would be better off without me.” They leave me shaken, because I don’t want to leave my baby; I just want the awful feelings to stop.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: joy seems out of reach, laughter forced, and even small pleasures like a quiet shower or a friend's meme feel flat. Each day brings a swirl of self-blame, sudden panicky awakenings, and tears that arrive without warning, while intrusive worries about your baby's safety race through your mind. Despite loving your infant deeply, you feel as though you're drowning in ordinary tasks and sometimes hear fleeting, frightening thoughts that everyone might be better off if you weren't here.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 28, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh naturally, matching "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes a near-complete loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "a lot of the time" and gives multiple daily examples, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily intrusive worries about infant safety without real cause, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden nighttime panic attacks with intense fear, physical symptoms, and catastrophic thinking, matching 'Yes, quite a lot</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to execute basic tasks, and feeling "drowning," matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to persistent anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness, spontaneous crying, and guilt—semantically aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent passive suicidal ideation ("crossed my mind once or twice") with distressing intrusive thoughts, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS score of 28/30 exceeds the 14-point cutoff for urgent referral; item 10 indicates self-harm thoughts. The constellation of <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>functional impairment</sym> lasting most of the day, nearly every day, aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>OB-GYN</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or local perinatal psychiatry service
2. Call a crisis line or 988 (US) if thoughts of self-harm intensify, or go to the nearest emergency department for safety assessment
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and help with overnight baby care until professional support is in place
4. Begin gentle scheduling: aim for one 3-4 hour block of sleep in 24 hours-accept help with night feeds or use pumped milk/formula
5. Try a 5-minute outdoor walk daily; sunlight and movement can modestly ease <sym>depressive symptoms</sym>
6. Limit information overload: choose one reputable parenting source and mute anxiety-provoking social media
7. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 28: Brief postpartum screening (Edinburgh PPD scale items)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, daily tearfulness
- Excessive self-blame, low self-worth (“everything is my fault”)
- Intrusive, catastrophic worries about infant safety
- Panic attacks during night‐waking, autonomic arousal
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, sense of “drowning”
- Initial insomnia, restless hypervigilance
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan/intent reported)

Pattern: Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, for ≥2 wks; interfere with functioning.

Screening significance: High concern for major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; safety risk flagged due to self-harm thoughts.

Recommendation: Refer for urgent psychiatric evaluation, consider formal EPDS scoring, facilitate safety plan and supports.
